doc.title: Ray Bauduc and Nappy Lamare Interview, 1959-09-09

title: Ray on Dixieland not being two-beat
summary: Ray says Dixieland is not truly two-beat. Metronome and Down Beat labeled it that to contrast with Benny Goodman's four-beat. He accents the second and fourth beats lightly and uses the sock cymbal for the afterbeat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I listened to him on those records. There's one thing I wanted to ask Ray was telling us the other night, if we don't take all your intermission either, but a little bit about the... a little bit about the two beat, like we were talking about down beat again, and the Crosby period saying that all Dixieland is two beat rhythm. And you were explaining the other night that that's the wrong idea. Oh, well, it isn't the wrong idea.

It's just that everybody has the idea that Dixieland is a two beat rhythm. And that that was brought out. The fact that music came along and progressed a little bit as far as when Benny Goodman came in, he kept a full beat ride. Yeah. And the magazine, like the Metronome and the down beat, they came along and they didn't know how to decipher Dixieland. So they called it two beat and Benny Goodman's style was four beat. Yeah. But as far as Dixieland, the actual beat of Dixieland to me is not two beat. It's on the second and the fourth beat accented. Very lightly. It isn't a oom-ching or nothing like that. Yeah. It's actually accented on the second and the fourth beat of the bar. And, well, I play a sick of patience and I'll play two beats, four beats and mix it up. But all the time I'm doing things like that, I try and keep a little after beat, what we call after beat, accent with my left hand or whatever hand that I'm using for that.
If you're a sock cymbal, do you use that for your...
I use that. I do that quite a bit. I mean, I always try and keep an after beat with the sock cymbal too.
